# Countability Axioms
## Definition 1
**(i)** A space $X$ is said to be ***first-countable*** if it has a countable [local basis](../Basis_Topology/index.qmd#sec-definition-3) at every $x \in X$.

**(ii)** A space $X$ is said to be ***second-countable*** if it has a countable [basis](../Basis_Topology/index.qmd#sec-definition-1).

### Remark 1
**(i)** Every metrizable space is first-countable.

::: {.callout-note title="Proof" icon=false collapse="true"}
Let $X$ be a metrizable space with a metric $d$ inducing the topology of $X$. For $x \in X$, define $\mathscr{B}_x := \left\{ B_d \left(x, \frac{1}{n} \right) \,\, \Bigg \vert \,\, n \in \mathbb{N} \right\}$. For an open set $U$ containing $x$, there exists $\delta > 0$ such that $B_d(x, \delta) \subset U$. Choosing $n \in \mathbb{N}$ such that $\frac{1}{n} < \delta$, we have

$$x \in B_d \left( x, \frac{1}{n} \right) \subset B_d(x, \delta) \subset U.$$

Hence, $\mathscr{B}_x$ is a countable local basis at $x$, so $X$ is first-countable. $\blacksquare$
:::

**(ii)** Every second-countable space is first-countable.

::: {.callout-note title="Proof" icon=false collapse="true"}
Let $X$ be a second-countable space with a countable basis $\mathscr{B}$. Since $\mathscr{B}_x := \{ B_x \in \mathscr{B} \mid x \in B_x \}$ is a local basis at each point $x \in X$ and $\mathscr{B}_x$ is countable, $X$ has a countable local basis at each point $x \in X$, so $X$ is first-countable. $\blacksquare$
:::

### Example 1
**(i)** $(\mathbb{R}, \mathscr{T}_{f})$ is neither first-countable nor second-countable.

::: {.callout-note title="Proof" icon=false collapse="true"}
Suppose that it is first-countable. Let $\mathscr{B}_x = \{ B_n \}_{n=1}^\infty$ be a countable local basis at $x$. (If $\mathscr{B}_x$ is finite, so $\mathscr{B}_x = \{ B_1, B_2, \dots, B_n \}$, then we let $B_n = B_{n+1} = B_{n+2} = \cdots$.) Since $(\mathbb{R}, \mathscr{T}_{f})$ is $T_1$, $\displaystyle \bigcap_{n=1}^\infty B_n = \{ x \}$. Note that

$$\mathbb{R} \setminus \{ x \} = \mathbb{R} \setminus \bigcap_{n=1}^\infty B_n = \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty (\mathbb{R} \setminus B_n).$$

Since each $B_n$ is open in $(\mathbb{R}, \mathscr{T}_{f})$, $\mathbb{R} \setminus B_n$ is a finite subset of $\mathbb{R}$. Thus, $\mathbb{R} \setminus \{ x \}$ is a countable union of finite sets, which is impossible. Hence, $(\mathbb{R}, \mathscr{T}_{f})$ is not first-countable, and hence not second-countable.
:::

**(ii)** $(\mathbb{R}, \mathscr{T}_{\text{discrete}})$ is first-countable, but not second-countable.

::: {.callout-note title="Proof" icon=false collapse="true"}
For $x \in \mathbb{R}$, the set $\{ \{ x \} \}$ is a countable local basis, so $(\mathbb{R}, \mathscr{T}_{\text{discrete}})$ is first-countable. On the other hand, suppose that there is a countable basis $\mathscr{B}$. For an open set $\{ x \}$, there is a basis element $B \in \mathscr{B}$ such that $x \in B \subset \{ x \}$. That is, $B$ must contain every singleton $\{ x \}$ in $\mathbb{R}$. Then $B$ contains an uncountable number of sets, which is a contradiction. Thus, $(\mathbb{R}, \mathscr{T}_{\text{discrete}})$ is not second-countable.
:::

**(iii)** $(\mathbb{R}, \mathscr{T}_{\text{usual}})$ is second-countable.

::: {.callout-note title="Proof" icon=false collapse="true"}
$\big[ (\because)$ $\{ (a, b) \mid a, b \in \mathbb{Q}, a < b \}$ is a countable basis.$\big]$
:::

## Theorem 1
Let $X$ be a first-countable space.

**(i)** Let $A \subset X$. Then there exists a sequence $\{ x_n \}$ in $A$ such that $\displaystyle \lim_{n \to \infty} x_n = x$ $\iff$ $x \in \bar{A}$.

**(ii)** Let $f: X \to Y$ be a function. Then $f$ is continuous $\iff$ for any sequence $\{ x_n \}$ in $X$ such that $\displaystyle \lim_{n \to \infty} x_n = x$, we have $\displaystyle \lim_{n \to \infty} f(x_n) = f(x)$.

거리 공간에서 성립하는 정리로 등장했지만, 실은 거리 공간이 제1 가산 공간이다보니 성립하는 내용이었다. 국소기저의 정의를 잘 생각해보면 굳이 외우지 않아도 자연스럽게 납득되는 내용들이다.

## Theorem 2
**(i)** A subspace of a first-countable (second-countable) space is first-countable (second-countable).

**(ii)** A countable product of first-countable (second-countable) spaces is first-countable (second-countable).

### Proof
**(i)** Let $A$ be a subspace of a space $X$. Suppose that $X$ is fisrt-countable. Let $x \in A$. Since $x \in X$, there is a countable local basis $\mathscr{B}_x$ at $x$. We claim that the set $\mathscr{U}_x = \{ B \cap A \mid B \in \mathscr{B}_x \}$ is a countable local basis for $A$ at $x$, so $A$ is first-countable.

$\big[ (\because)$ Since each $B$ in $\mathscr{B}_x$ contains $x$, each so does $B \cap A$. Let $U$ be an open subset of $A$ containing $x$. Then $U = V \cap A$ for some open subset $V$ of $X$. Since $V$ contains $x$, we have $x \in B \subset V$ for some $B \in \mathscr{B}_x$, which implies that $x \in B \cap A \subset V \cap A = U$. Hence, $\mathscr{U}_x$ is a local basis for $A$ at $x$. Since $\mathscr{B}_x$ is countable, so is $\mathscr{U}_x. \big]$

In this case, suppose that $X$ is second-countable, which means that there is a countable basis $\mathscr{B}$. Then $\mathscr{B}' = \{ B \cap A \mid B \in \mathscr{B} \}$ is a countable basis for $A$, which means that $A$ is second-countable.

**(ii)** Let $\{ X_\alpha \}_{\alpha \in J}$ be a countable collection of spaces $X_\alpha$. Note that $\displaystyle X := \prod_{\alpha \in J} X_\alpha$ is equipped with the product topology. Suppose that each $X_\alpha$ is first-countable.

Let $x = (x_\alpha)_{\alpha \in J} \in X$. Since each $X_\alpha$ is first-countable, there is a countable local basis $\mathscr{B}_\alpha$ for $X_\alpha$ at $x_\alpha$. For a finite subset $I$ of the index set $J$, we define

$$C^I_x = \left\{ B_x = \prod_{\alpha \in J} B_\alpha \,\, \Bigg \vert \,\, \begin{cases} B_\alpha \in \mathscr{B}_\alpha & \text{if } \alpha \in I \\ B_\alpha = X_\alpha & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} \right\}.$$

Since $I$ is finite and each $\mathscr{B}_\alpha$ is countable, each $C^I_x$ is countable. Then the set

$$\mathscr{B}_x = \bigcup_{I \subset J, \vert I \vert < \infty} C^I_x$$

is also countable, because the number of $I$ is countable. We will show that $\mathscr{B}_x$ is a local basis for $X$ at $x$.

Note that each $B_x \in C^I_x$ is an open subset of $X$ containing $x$. Let $U$ be an open subset of $X$ containing $x$. Then $x \in B \subset U$ for some basis element $B = \prod_{\alpha \in J} U_\alpha$ of $X$ where $U_\alpha$ is an open subset of $X_\alpha$ if $\alpha \in I^\ast$ and $U_\alpha = X_\alpha$ if $\alpha \in J \setminus I^\ast$, for some finite set $I^\ast \subset J$. For each $\alpha \in I^\ast$, we have that $x_\alpha \in B_\alpha \subset U_\alpha$ for some $B_\alpha \in \mathscr{B}_\alpha$. Then the element

$$B_x = \prod_{\alpha \in J} C_\alpha$$

where $C_\alpha = B_\alpha$ if $\alpha \in I^\ast$ and $C_\alpha = X_\alpha$ if $\alpha \in J \setminus I^\ast$ belongs to $C^{I^\ast}_x$, which means $B_x \in \mathscr{B}_x$ and $x \in B_x \subset U$. Hence, $\mathscr{B}_x$ is a local basis for $X$ at $x$, so $X$ is first-countable.

On the other hand, we suppose that each $X_\alpha$ is second-countable, so there is a countable basis $\mathscr{B}_\alpha$ for each $X_\alpha$. For a finite subset $I$ of the index set $J$, we define

$$C_I = \left\{ \prod_{\alpha \in J} B_\alpha \,\, \Bigg \vert \,\, \begin{cases} B_\alpha \in \mathscr{B}_\alpha & \text{if } \alpha \in I \\ B_\alpha = X_\alpha & \text{otherwise} \end{cases} \right\}.$$

Since $I$ is finite and each $\mathscr{B}_\alpha$ is countable, each $C_I$ is countable. Then the set

$$\mathscr{B} = \bigcup_{I \subset J, \vert I \vert < \infty} C_I$$

is a countable basis for $X$, because the number of $I$ is countable. Hence, $X$ is second-countable. $\blacksquare$

# Dense, Lindelöf, and Separable
## Definition 2
Let $X$ be a topological space.

**(i)** A subset $S$ of $X$ is said to be ***dense*** if $\overline{S} = X$.

**(ii)** $X$ is called a ***Lindelöf space*** if every open cover of $X$ has a countable subcover.

**(iii)** $X$ is said to be ***separable*** if it has a countable dense subset.

### Example 2
**(i)** $(\mathbb{R}, \mathscr{T}_{\text{usual}})$ is NOT compact, but is Lindelöf and separable.

::: {.callout-note title="Proof" icon=false collapse="true"}
Since $\mathscr{B} = \{ (a, b) \mid a < b, a, b \in \mathbb{Q} \}$ is a countable basis, $(\mathbb{R}, \mathscr{T}_{\text{usual}})$ is second-countable, so it is Lindelöf and separable.
:::

**(ii)** $(\mathbb{R}, \mathscr{T}_{\text{discrete}})$ is neither Lindelöf nor separable.

::: {.callout-note title="Proof" icon=false collapse="true"}
Since the open cover $\{ \{x \} \mid x \in \mathbb{R} \}$ does not have a countable subcover, $(\mathbb{R}, \mathscr{T}_{\text{discrete}})$ is not Lindelöf.

Suppose that $(\mathbb{R}, \mathscr{T}_{\text{discrete}})$ has a countable dense subset $S$. Since $S$ is closed, $S = \overline{S}$. However, we have $S = \overline{S} = \mathbb{R}$. Thus, $\vert S \vert = \vert \mathbb{R} \vert$, which contradicts that $S$ is countable. Hence, $(\mathbb{R}, \mathscr{T}_{\text{discrete}})$ is not separable.
:::

**(iii)** $(\mathbb{R}, \mathscr{T}_{\text{usual}}) \times (\mathbb{R}, \mathscr{T}_{\text{usual}})$ is Lindelöf.

::: {.callout-note title="Proof" icon=false collapse="true"}
Note that 

$$\bigcup_{n=1}^\infty ([-n, n] \times [-n, n]) = \mathbb{R}^2.$$

Let $\mathcal{U}$ be an open cover of $\mathbb{R}^2$. Since $[-n, n] \times [-n, n]$ is covered by $\mathcal U$, there is a subcollection $\mathcal{U}_n$ of $\mathcal{U}$ that covers $[-n, n] \times [-n, n]$. Since $[-n, n] \times [-n, n]$ is compact, there is a finite subcover $\mathcal{U}_n^\ast$. Let $\mathcal{U}^\ast = \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty \mathcal{U}_n^\ast$. Then we have

$$\mathbb{R}^2 = \bigcup_{n=1}^\infty ([-n, n] \times [-n, n]) = \bigcup_{U \in \mathcal{U}^\ast} U.$$

Thus $\mathcal{U}$ has a countable subcover, so $\mathbb{R}^2$ is Lindelöf.
:::

## Remark 2
**(i)** The product of Lindelöf spaces is not necessarily Lindelöf.

::: {.callout-note title="Proof" icon=false collapse="true"}
Note that $\mathbb{R}_\ell$ is second-countable because $\mathscr{B} = \{ [a, b) \mid a, b \in \mathbb{Q} \}$ is a countable basis. Hence $\mathbb{R}_\ell$ is Lindelöf.

Consider $\mathbb{R}_\ell \times \mathbb{R}_\ell = \mathbb{R}_\ell^2$, called the ***Sorgenfrey plane***. The space $\mathbb{R}_\ell^2$ has a basis of the form $[a, b) \times [c, d)$.

Note that $L := \{ (x, -x) \mid x \in \mathbb{R} \}$ is a closed subset of $\mathbb{R}_\ell^2$, because $\mathbb{R}_\ell^2 - L$ is open. Then $\mathcal{U} = \{ \mathbb{R}_\ell^2 - L \} \cup \{ [a, b) \times [-a, c) \mid a, b, c \in \mathbb{R}\}$ is an open cover of $\mathbb{R}_\ell^2$. Since $L$ is uncountable and each $[a, b) \times [-a, c)$ has at most one element of $L$, $\mathcal{U}$ cannot have a finite subcover. Thus, $\mathbb{R}_\ell^2$ is not Lindelöf.
:::

**(ii)** The subspace of a Lindelöf space is not necessarily Lindelöf.

::: {.callout-note title="Proof" icon=false collapse="true"}
Consider $\mathscr{T} = \{ U \subset \mathbb{R} \mid U = \mathbb{R} \text{ or } 0 \notin U \}$. Then $\mathscr{T}$ is a topology on $X$.

Let $\mathcal{U}$ be an open cover of $(\mathbb{R}, \mathscr{T})$. Since $0$ should be convered by $\mathcal{U}$, $\mathbb{R} \in \mathcal{U}$, which means that $\{ \mathbb{R} \}$ is a finite subcover of $\mathcal{U}$. Hence $(\mathbb{R}, \mathscr{T})$ is compact, so is Lindelöf.

Let $Y = \mathbb{R} \setminus \{ 0 \}$ be a subspace of $(\mathbb{R}, \mathscr{T})$. Since any subset $S$ of $Y$ does not contain $0$, $S$ is open in $Y$, which means that the topology of $Y$ is a discrete topology. Hence, $Y$ is not Lindelöf.
:::

## Theorem 3
**(i)** A second-countable space is a Lindelöf space.

**(ii)** A second-countable space is separable.

### Proof
Let $X$ be a second-countable space. Then $X$ has a countable basis $\mathscr{B}$. Since $\mathscr{B}$ is countable, we can denote $\mathscr{B} = \{ B_n \}_{n \in \Lambda}$ for some subset $\Lambda$ of $\mathbb{N}$.

**(i)** Let $\mathcal{U}$ be an open cover of $X$. For each $n \in \Lambda$ for which it is possible, we choose an open set $U_n \in \mathcal{U}$ such that $B_n \subset U_n$. We denote the collection of the chosen sets $U_n$ by $\mathcal{U}^\ast$. Note that we can choose at least one $U_n$ because each open set $U \in \mathcal{U}$ contains a basis element $B_n \in \mathscr{B}$. Since $\Lambda$ is countable, so is $\mathcal{U}^\ast$. We will show that $\mathcal{U}^\ast$ covers $X$.

Let $x \in X$. Then $x \in U$ for some $U \in \mathcal{U}$, and $x \in B_n \subset U$ for some $B_n \in \mathscr{B}$. Then there is an element $U_n \in \mathcal{U}^\ast$ such that $x \in B_n \subset U_n$, which means that $\mathcal{U}^\ast$ covers $X$. Hence, $\mathcal{U}$ has a countable subcover $\mathcal{U}^\ast$, so $X$ is a Lindelöf space.

**(ii)** For each nonempty $B_n \in \mathscr{B}$, we choose $x_n \in B_n$ and construct $D = \{ x_n \}$. Since $\Lambda$ is countable, so is $D$. We claim that $\overline{D} = X$.

Let $x \in X$, and let $B$ be a basis element of $\mathscr{B}$ containing $x$. Then $B \cap D$ contains $x_n$, so it is nonempty. Thus, $x \in \overline{D}$, which means $\overline{D} = X$, so $D$ is a countable dense subset of $X$. $\blacksquare$
